title: Compare UK Card Machine Providers Side by Side
description: SumUp, Square, PayPal POS (Zettle), Dojo, Teya, takepayments, Worldpay, Barclaycard, Lloyds Cardnet and more compared: fees, contracts and hardware.
intro: The main card machine and payment terminal providers in the UK, grouped by how they charge. Published rates are shown with the date we checked them. Everything else is quoted, so get a written quote and summary box before you sign.

blocks.title: Card machine providers
blocks.intro: Filter by pricing model. Cards are listed alphabetically within each group, not ranked. Links go to each provider’s own website. Rates are for in-person UK card payments as published in October 2026: always check the current fee schedule.

items.title: PayPal Point of Sale (Zettle)
items.text: Zettle by PayPal is being renamed PayPal Point of Sale. Flat-rate card reader and POS app with no contract or recurring fees, popular with small shops and market traders.
specs: Reader from £29 (new users), Terminal from £149, ex VAT

items.title: Revolut Business
items.text: Revolut Business customers can take in-person payments with Tap to Pay on iPhone in the Revolut Business app or with Revolut’s own card reader. Fees depend on your Revolut plan.
specs: Set by your Revolut Business plan
iPhone (Tap to Pay) or Revolut Reader

items.title: Square
items.text: All-in-one payments and free POS software, with paid plans for restaurants, retail and appointments. No setup or monthly fee on the Free plan.

items.title: SumUp
items.text: Low-cost readers and terminals with no monthly fee on pay as you go, plus an optional Payments Plus subscription with a lower headline rate. Also sells POS systems (including the former Goodtill).

items.title: Dojo
items.text: Card machines, pay-at-table and booking tools aimed at hospitality and retail, from the company formerly known for the Paymentsense brand. Rates vary by card type and are quoted per business.
specs: Personal quote; rates by card type
Monthly terminal fee; see Dojo’s fee schedule
Fast payouts, pay at table, EPOS integrations

items.title: Elavon
items.text: One of the UK’s largest card acquirers, owned by U.S. Bancorp. Works with many EPOS and terminal partners, typically for established and multi-site businesses.

items.title: takepayments
items.text: Stockport-based card machine provider and part of Global Payments. Packages are built per business; you also hold an agreement with a nominated acquiring bank.

items.title: Teya
items.text: Card machines with built-in 4G and Wi-Fi, a business account with cashback and cash advances. Teya says it has no standard price list and tailors rates to each business.
specs: +0.10% if paid out to an external bank

items.title: Worldpay
items.text: One of the UK’s biggest card acquirers, now owned by Global Payments (deal completed 12 January 2026). Offers card machines for small businesses and enterprise payment processing.

items.title: Barclaycard Payments
items.text: Barclays’ card acceptance business. Its range includes Smartpay Anywhere (a mobile reader with no contract) and contract terminals such as Smartpay Touch and Flex.
specs: Approval depends on your business’s finances

items.title: Lloyds Cardnet
items.text: Lloyds Banking Group’s card acquirer. Offers a pay-as-you-go mobile reader (mPOS) as well as countertop and portable terminals on bespoke pricing.

items.title: Tyl by NatWest
items.text: NatWest Group’s card payments service for UK businesses, with card machines, online payments and Tap to Pay on iPhone. Also offered through Royal Bank of Scotland and Ulster Bank.

sections.h2: Pay as you go or contract?
sections.html:
UK card machine providers fall into two camps:

  • Pay as you go (flat rate): you buy a reader once and pay a fixed percentage per sale, with no monthly fee and no contract. SumUp, Square, PayPal Point of Sale and Lloyds Cardnet’s mPOS reader work this way. Simple and predictable, and usually cheapest for lower volumes.
  • Quoted / contract: you rent a terminal for a monthly fee and get rates set for your business, often varying by card type, sometimes with authorisation fees. Dojo, Teya, takepayments, Worldpay, Elavon and the banks’ terminal plans work this way. Busier businesses with larger average sales can often pay less overall, but you must read the whole price.

As a rough guide, once your monthly card takings reach a few thousand pounds, it’s worth getting quotes. Our fees guide shows how to compare a flat rate with a quote, and this worked example shows when a subscription plan pays off.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before you sign
sections.html:
1. What is my rate for each card type, and is there an authorisation fee per transaction?
  2. What is the monthly terminal fee, and is the terminal rented, leased or bought?
  3. How long is the minimum term, and what does it cost to leave early?
  4. Are there PCI compliance fees, minimum monthly service charges or account fees?
  5. When do payouts arrive, and do I need to use your business account?
  6. Does the terminal integrate with my EPOS system?

Large acquirers must give small businesses a standard summary box of prices. Ask for it, and compare like with like: see how to read a card machine quote.

Several well-known brands share an owner, which can matter when you switch:

  • Global Payments owns Worldpay (since January 2026) and takepayments.
  • PayPal owns Zettle, now being renamed PayPal Point of Sale.
  • Block owns Square.
  • Fiserv owns Clover, an EPOS and payments platform sold through partners.
  • Dojo is the trading brand of the company previously known as Paymentsense.

faqs.q: Which card machine is best for a small business?
faqs.a: For low or variable takings, a pay-as-you-go reader with no monthly fee is usually the simplest and cheapest place to start. As takings grow, compare quotes from contract providers and look at subscription plans like SumUp Payments Plus. See card machine fees.

faqs.q: Is SumUp cheaper than Square or Zettle?
faqs.a: On published pay-as-you-go rates for in-person UK cards, SumUp’s 1.69% is slightly lower than the 1.75% charged by Square and PayPal Point of Sale (October 2026). Hardware prices, software, payout speed and extra fees also matter, so compare the whole package.

faqs.q: Why don’t some providers publish their prices?
faqs.a: Contract providers such as Dojo, Teya and the big acquirers usually price each business individually, based on turnover, sector, average sale and card mix. Ask for a written quote and the standard summary box.
